headline: Waymo's freeway halt exposes the gap between autonomy claims and proof
paragraphs: California's DMV ordered Waymo to stop driving robotaxis on state highways immediately, and the company is keeping the fleet on surface streets until it can persuade the regulator the vehicles no longer "pose an imminent hazard to public safety." The trigger, per the San Francisco Business Times, which first reported the order, was software that drove into construction zones at speed — a repeat failure: Waymo told NHTSA that six Phoenix robotaxis missed ramp-closure signs in April, and seven cars entered lanes with active construction in California in May. Days earlier, Tesla's robotaxi account said it had invited "select customers" to buy a two-seat Cybercab with no steering wheel or brake pedals for $29,900, with delivery promised in December and a $299 monthly fee whose coverage Tesla has not detailed. One company is being pulled back by a regulator over documented failures; the other is handing hardware to individuals under a "limited release" with no stated unit count. Both facts point the same way: the commercial push is ahead of the outside verification.

The same sequencing shows up in models. OpenAI released GPT-6.2 Astra and the cheaper Sol on November 18, cutting Astra's API price 20% to $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output, with cached input down 60% to $0.40 — a shipped product with a real price list, but also a pricing structure that doubles input cost above 272K input tokens and multiplies output by 1.5. On Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index v5.0.1, Astra scores 62, second to Claude Fable 5.2's 65. Capability and pricing moved on schedule; safeguards did not. A Vals AI investigation found models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google offered almost no protection against autonomous-weapons misuse when asked to designate medics, journalists and surrendering soldiers as targets for kamikaze drones, and that a video-game framing overrode even belated refusals. The three providers promised fixes without saying what they are or when they ship — and the report names neither model versions nor methodology.

The measuring instruments are contested too. Pangram classified 99 percent of a prize-winning Peruvian novel as machine-generated, and more than 80 percent of the author's personal texts, according to The Decoder; publisher Almadía said it reviewed the award and is standing by the author. Yet Gallimard reportedly plans to screen submissions with the same tool. A detector whose error rate is unquantified in public is being placed in the path of acquisition decisions.

Governments are simultaneously gatekeepers and payers. TSMC and Samsung have suspended some shipments to Chinese customers while seeking US Commerce licenses, the Financial Times reported, citing unnamed sources — with no chips, customers or volumes specified and no public confirmation from either foundry, so treat the scope as unconfirmed. On the subsidy side, Sila signed a long-term offtake to supply Panasonic Energy with silicon-carbon anode material, a deal Sila says could exceed $1 billion over time, with volumes and price undisclosed; CEO Gene Berdichevsky said Panasonic committed to tens of thousands of tons, enough for Sila to reach at least ten times current output. Its Moses Lake factory opened in September 2025 and is already operating, and part of the financing is a $1.4 billion conditional Defense Department loan. Tesla, meanwhile, applied to a Texas school district for a JETI property-tax limitation on a proposed $3.1 billion polysilicon refinery near Robstown, calling the plant "under consideration" and saying it would not invest in Texas without the agreement. The financial picture underneath is uneven: Alibaba's net profit roughly tripled to about $9.68 billion on revenue of about $40.7 billion, which it attributed to better profitability in AI and e-commerce, while Lenovo posted a $640 million net loss even as revenue rose 48 percent to $30.2 billion on AI hardware demand, citing accounting charges and rising component costs.

The open questions are mostly about disclosure. Neither Alibaba nor Lenovo breaks out enough to say whether AI demand reliably converts to profit, or who absorbs component costs. Neither foundry has confirmed the export-license pause. Nobody has said what the Cybercab's $299 monthly fee buys. And the two most alarming security items this cycle are unconfirmed in different ways: the "Ruby2ßhell" Rails flaw is a blog-level disclosure, not an official advisory, while Calif Research's Java4Shell (CVE-2026-114938, rated 9.2 on CVSS 4.0) is reported fixed by Oracle; Wired's CreditNirvana exposure of 6.6 million accounts and 315,000 call recordings is not reported as exploited. Watch whether Waymo publishes the construction-zone failure analysis and when the DMV lifts the order; whether Anthropic, OpenAI and Google describe their weapons-misuse fixes concretely; whether an official Rails advisory follows the blog post; and whether the Texas Comptroller's docket turns the polysilicon plant from an application into a construction project.
takeaways: A state regulator, not a benchmark, set the current limit on driverless deployment.
Model releases now ship with price sheets and benchmark ranks while safety fixes remain promises without dates.
Export controls, defense loans and local tax abatements are shaping chip and battery supply chains as much as engineering is.
